The great influx of population into our North-western territories and the very large additional areas of fertile land which are being brought under cultivation combine to further press upon us the need for increased transportation facilities for the forwarding of our grain and other products to the markets of the world, through Canadian channels. The whole question of transportation and terminal facilities continues to occupy much attention, and my government will immediately appoint a commission of experienced men to report on the subject.
This statement in the speech from the Throne was based, as the colleagues of the Prime Minister well know, on the Order in Council which has been read by the leader of the opposition this afternoon, which gives in detail the reasons which satisfied the colleagues of the Premier, which satisfied the Crown, and which was intended to satisfy this House and the country, that the pressing question of the hour was a transportation commission in order to investigate the complex and complicated subject which had been engrossing, and which was to continue to engross their attention. Surely, in the face of all that, we might have expected some one minister if not more, to have pointed out the extraordinary circumstances under which this Bill was conceived, and the slight probability there was that this country would secure its rights in such an agreement. Let me call attention to the fact that although this agreement) was made between some gentlemen representing the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and the government, the agreement will be wholly inoperative, and we are wasting our time discussing it, unless the Grand Trunk Railway, which is in no way at present bound by it, will come forward and carry out the engagement which these gentlemen have made for it. What are we to think of the contract made by the Premier with gentlemen, one of whom stated to a meeting of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway in the motherland a few months ago, that they were about to enter into an undertaking which would

never in any respect cost them one dol- I lar or jeopardize one dollar of their property ? What are we to think of a bargain of such a character, that the government itself cannot be certain that the Grand Trunk Railway shareholders at their next meeting will ratify it and yet we are spending a month here discussing the matter, and relying solely on the Grand Trunk Railway Company being willing to carry out a contract to which at present they are not parties. No more conclusive evidence can be given of the one-sidedness of the bargain, of the advantage on one hand and the disadvantage on the other, (the country of course being at a disadvantage), than the simple fact that both the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and the representatives of the government were perfectly satisfied without any guarantee except the inherent nature of the contract itself, that the Grand Trunk shareholders will ratify such a bargain. When we come to look at this contract, we on this side of the House, and I ought to be able to say, gentlemen supporting the treasury benches as well, are entitled to say to the government :	Surely you had some reasons
to justify such a contract as this.
Well, Sir, the Prime Minister did give his reasons. Far be it from me to say that in his long and eloquent speech no reasons were adduced. I have gone through the speech of the Prime Minister carefully and I have collated his reasons, and I shall state them to the House. I ask the House to say whether in a case such as this, we should not first consider whether the reasons given for such a measure are or are not founded in fact. If they are not founded in fact we are surely justified in refusing to support the measure, and if they are founded in fact then the next consideration would be :	Will the effect of
them be as represented ? In looking over those reasons given by the Prime Minister, I think I can fairly ask of hon. gentlemen opposite if they honestly in their hearts believe that these reasons are sufficient justification for their supporting such a measure as this ? These are the reasons given by the Prime Minister :	That the
construction of this road was a national and commercial necessity ; that the construction must be immediate ; that it must be from Moncton to the Pacific ocean ; that it will not parallel the Intercolonial Railway ; that you must keep control of the road ; that we must be safe from the bonding privileges ; that we used American ports because we had no railways to reach our own ports, and that we had to keep control so as to regulate the traffic. These were the reasons given by the right hon. gentleman, as those which led the government to introduce this measure. Now, let me in a few words take these reasons one by one. I have enumerated them together so that hon. gentlemen
may have an opportunity, if they see fit, to compare the Prime Minister's reasons as I have stated them, with the reasons set forth in: his speech and I am sure they will not find one reason given in that speech beyond those I have mentioned. The first reason given is that this is a national and commercial necessity. I am free to admit that the expression ' national necessity ' is rather a euphoneous phrase. One naturally feels an almost instinctive yearning for anything that is a national necessity, and so I suppose hon. gentlemen opposite are ready to jump at once to secure for themselves and their constituents in Quebec a national necessity. But after all, when we come down to facts ; when we lay aside the gems of oratory and come down to the level of hard facts, does any one of the supporters of the Prime Minister believe that the construction of this road from Moncton to Winnipeg and from Winnipeg to the Pacific is a national necessity ? Is there a gentleman in this House who does not know that we are a nation, that we have been a nation ever since the happy morning the Prime Minister awoke to find that somehow he had made us a nation. We have the best authority for knowing that we are a nation ; but we have existed without this road so far. Is there a single man in this House or in this country to-night, so blind to all sense of reason, that he can face his fellowman and say honestly to him, that this road is such a national necessity that we cannot as a nation exist without it ?
Then, if it is not a national necessity, is it a commercial necessity ? In what possible sense can it be a commercial necessity ? Why, Sir, if this road be a commercial necessity and a national necessity, heaven defend us, for we will not be a nation during the six or seven years that it is being built. We, must cease to be a nation ; we must be swallowed up by the adjoining republic or submerged beneath the waves ; some dreadful fate must be' ours if this is a national or commercial necessity, for we cannot have it for six or seven years. Does not every one know that when the right hon. the Prime Minister spoke of this as being a national and comipercial necessity that he was merely using a high-sounding euphoneous expression which was not warranted by the facts.
Then the Prime Minister told us that the construction must ]be< immediate :	that
there was no time to wait for surveys ; that he had no timel to wait for any more information than the government has on hand at the present moment. Why this extraordinary haste ? There was a time years ago when the country was bound to build the Intercolonial Railway : there was a time when this country entered into an agreement also to build the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the right hon. gentleman when he said that this road should be built

which will he in Winnipeg from three to five years before the eastern section reaches that city. It is perfectly clear that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will be in Winnipeg long before the eastern division reaches that spot. Had the agreement been drawn intelligently and in the interests of the country-and I am not blaming the Minister of Justice, because I presume he simply put the intentions of the parties in legal phraseology-it would have provided for the building of a line from Winipeg east from which a branch could be built to North Bay or to Port Arthur or Port William and thus secured the transportation of the products of the west by the lakes through our eastern ports. But instead we find the government making an arrangement which lays before the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway the temptation for years to come to send then- wheat south from Winnipeg across the border, through to Chicago and Duluth, and we know that it is one of the hardest things in the world, once traffic has taken a certain route, to divert it to another. . Had the government been more eager to look after the interests of the coun-trv and less anxious to make a bargain, we would have had a totally different arrangement submitted to 11s.
When my hon. friend the Minister of Finance came to discuss the question, he added very little to the reasons advanced by the First Minister. He pleaded that the Conservative party did not require surveys in 1871 before entering into a contract for building the Intercolonial Railway, nor did they require surveys before contracting to build the Canadian Pacific Railway. But the circumstances in these cases were entirely different from those which exist today. What were the facts when the Intercolonial Railway contract was entered into? That road, Sir, was a national necessity. Every one knows that the old provinces had been getting along so unhappily, every one knows that there was so much friction between them, owing to unhappy religious and racial difficulties, not fomented by the Conservative party, that it became necessary to do something ; and so the statesmen on both sides of politics agreed that Nova Scotia and New Brunswick should be added to the original Canadas and thus restore harmony by forming a confederation. There was therefore a national necessity for the building of the Intercolonial Railway. The lower provinces would not have come in unless they were promised a railway to connect with the upper provinces. Surely, if ever there was a case of national necessity which justified the conduct of the government, it was that one. But will anybody pretend that such a necessity now exists ? Then, when the contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway was entered upon, the question of building that road had been before the country for years. This country had pledged itself to British Columbia to build the Mr. NORTHRUP.
road, and again there was a national necessity. We had purchased the prairies of the west and we knew that extension to the Pacific was absolutely necessary for the Dominion. It was necessary for our national existence that we should build a railway across the prairies to connect with British Columbia ; and that being the case, we entered into the contract to build the Canadian Pacific Railway. But is there anything in the circumstances to-day which, in the most remote degree, resembles the circumstances of those days, when a real, true national necessity existed ?
A great deal of capital was sought to be made by the Finance Minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding) and the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) out of the charge that we had attacked, year after year, the management of the Intercolonial Railway. They stigmatized us as not being friends of the Intercolonial Railway. Well, Mr. Speaker, we have never attacked the Intercolonial Railway itself from this side, but have attacked, and will continue to attack, the management of that noble public work ; and when hon. gentlemen like my hon. friend the Minister of Finance actually deride us because we oppose grants for the construction of elevators at St. John and Halifax, we can easily turn ,ie tables on them by pointing to the fact that not a single bushel of grain has gone through the Halifax elevator and but one cargo and that at an expense to the country of $10,000, through the elevator at St. John, so that these two institutions are standing as costly monuments of the lavish expenditure of this government.
My hon. friend the Finance Minister, whose honesty every one on this side, I am sure, admits, has said-and I am certain he said it in all sincerity-that he had looked carefully through the Bill and thought it was an honest Bill, because he could not find anything in it for the promoters. I am quite willing to accept the assurance of the hon. gentleman. I think that about as near as he could get to finding out where the money was to be made would be to look through the pages of the Bill, and if he did not see dollar bills sticking out he would be unable to find anything in it for the promoters. But there are perhaps other people who have better ideas on that point. Just look at the position of the road. If hon. gentlemen opposite would lay aside their party prejudices and view the question upon its merits, I am perfectly certain that a mere statement of the position of the road would prevent the Bill being discussed five minutes. Just think of the position in which the country is to be placed. The country is to guarantee 75 per cent of the western section, and I shall say nothing of the ease with which a company could put in the whole cost under cover of the 75 per cent guarantee. The country bears all the cost, in the meantime, of the construction of the eastern division, so that when the road is completed, it is

perfectly clear that this country will owe $50,000,000 or $60,000,000 for the construction of the eastern division and will have guaranteed three-quarters the cost of the construction of the western division. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway have obtained their charter. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Heyd) asked me what the promoters of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway put into the road up to the time of its completion, and I told him that they did not put in one dollar, as I shall prove. Let us see whence the money comes. From Moncton to Winnipeg the government bear all the expense of construction. West of Winnipeg the government bears 75 per cent. That only leaves 25 per cent to be raised by the company. Whence does that come ? I confess it will be a little hard, from reading the Bill, to be perfectly certain just whence it does come. The language is so artfully changed in the c'ause providing for the 25 per cent to be guaranteed by the Grand Trunk as compared with the government guarantee of 75 per cent, that it is very hard to say what the meaning of the words may be. But the Minister of Finance and the Minister of the Interior both agree as to the meaning of that clause, and both say that the Grand Trunk Railway has to provide 25 per cent by guaranteeing sufficient bonds to raise that amount.
Now, if the government provide 75 per cent and the Grand Trunk is to guarantee bonds to raise the other 25 per cent, what is the Grand Trunk Pacific to put in? Your road is completed, and your company has. not paid a dollar. What, then, is the position of your company ? It has $20,000,000 of preferred stock and $25,000,000 of common stock, and there has not been a dollar put up for it. I suppose the Grand Trunk will get either the $20,000,000 or the $25,000,000 for guaranteeing the bonds. The balance will be divided, I suppose, among the intelligent, industrious and successful promoters. And if the Finance Minister were in that neighbourhood I fancy he would be able to form some idea where the dollar bills were. But we find the road completed, and the company has not put a dollar fnto it. And in this r appeal to the words of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of the Interior, who stated distinctly that the Grand Trunk is to guarantee, not the balance of the bonds, but enough of the bonds to make up the balance of the money. There will be quite a distinction between the two. It seems to me that the contract clause was such that nobody could say with certainty exactly what it meant. On the whole, I should thought it possible that under it the Grand Trunk would guarantee the bonds for the face value of 25 per cent and, if that was not sufficient, the shortage would be made up by the company in some other way. But when two of the gentlemen who made the contract, one of them the Finance Minister, who
must know if anybody knows, the meaning of the financial terms, tell us that the Grand Trunk is to raise the whole 25 per cent of the cost, we naturally ask where the Grand Trunk Pacific Company is going to put in a dollar.
Now, the Minister of Justice spent some time in discussing the question of equipment, and I take that up now, because it is germane to the question of who provides the money for the construction of the road. The hon. gentleman said that the meaning of section 22 and some other sections to which he referred, was cleat beyond per-adventure, so clear that no lawyer of the eminence of the ieader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) and the senior member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) should have dreamed of making such a statement as that the company was not bound to purchase the equipment to be provided for this eastern division. I venture to say that the statement made by the Minister of Justice has confirmed every member of the House who has taken the trouble to pay attention to the clause in the belief that the view expressed by the leader of the opposition and by the hon. senior member for Hamilton is absolutely accurate, and still more, that the Minister of Justice is afraid that it is so. Let us see what was done. The contract was drawn up by the Minister of Justice. Then counsel, Mr. Shepley, is ealled in. I wish to be understood as saying that Mr. Shepley is one of the ablest and most experienced and most painstaking counsel that the Minister of Justice could have secured. I hope it will not be thought for a moment that I am finding fault with that part of it. If Mr. Shepley received a rattling good fee, I for one will not criticise the estimate when it comes down. But, after he has revised the contract and it has been accepted, suddenly in this House a new idea Is sprung, and the minister goes back to his counsel and says : Do you mean to say you were such an idiot as to leave such a hole in the contract-
I did not suggest that he was an idiot.

I am merely putting it in extreme form. He asked the counsel if he thought he could have made such a blunder. If the Minister of Justice did not read to Mr. Shepley, the deputy minister, Mr. Newcombe, and to Mr. Gormully any more of the sections of the contract than he read here to-night, I should be sorry to say that they were wrong in the opinion they gave
Counsel generally read contracts before they give opinions in my country.

I should think so. But the opinion was such that I concluded that they could not have done so. The Minister of Justice' called our attention to

sections 11, 12, 13, 19, 22, 34, 35 and 37. In the majority of these sections, we find that all depends on the meaning of the word ' equip.' Now, ' equip ' is not a legal term. I am not aware of any legal work in which any legal meaning is attached to that word. I consulted several legal lexicons, and I do not find it mentioned. Consequently I take the Standard dictionary in order to find the ordinary meaning of this English word, and I find that the meaning of ' equip ' is given as ' To furnish or fit out for service, task or course ; provide with all that is necessary for a successful undertaking.' You will see that it is possible to provide with all necessary for a successful undertaking without purchasing. If the Minister of Justice, upon taking office under the Prime Minister were to say : I would like to secure a house ready furnished for my residence in Ottawa ; and the Prime Minister were to provide him with such a house, the Minister of Justice could hardly refuse to pay the rent on the ground that the furniture had been borrowed or leased- so long as it was not stolen. It would not be necessary that it should be purchased. Equip' is one thing ; purchase and equip is another thing. I should have thought under ordinary circumstances that when we find the word ' acquire ' used again and again in this contract-there are probably few words used in it so frequently-that in this case the Minister of Justice would have it read ' acquire and equip ' or ' purchase and equip.' Then, we should know where we were. The other clauses the minister read did not take the matter a*particle further. They merely repeat the use of the word ' equip.' We do not find that it means that the company* shall purchase and equip. Then, we come to section 14, which the minister did not read to this House. Let me take the liberty of reading the 14th clause to the House, and then I will ask if there is a layman in this House who cannot at a glance see the meaning of the word ' equip ' as used in this contract. This clause, 14, provides for the working expenditure. And hon. gentlemen will remember that, for the first ten years the expenditure is to be deducted before the rental is paid. So, it is important to know what the working expenditure is. On the eastern division they can take certain things for working expenditure. This is the clause:
For the purposes of this agreement, the expression * working expenditure ' as applied to the eastern division of the railway, shall mean and include all expenses of maintenance of the said division, and of the stations, buildings, works and conveniences belonging thereto, and of the rolling and other stock and movable plant used in the working thereof, and all such tolls, rents or annual sums as are paid in respect of property leased to, or held by, the company

They have some leased property. That is admitted. Now, I will call the minister's attention to what follows :

-in respect of the said eastern division (apart from the rent of any other leased line), or in respect of the hire of rolling stock let to the company as part of the equipment of the said eastern division.
Can the English language be plainer ? Here is an agreement by which $5,000,000 of rolling stock is to be provided-not purchased-for the equipment of that road. It is marked; as assigned and set apart for that division ; I suppose in order that if it slips off to any other it can be brought back, and, on the average, the value of rolling stock shall be $5,000,000. There is no doubt that the value of the rolling stock is to be $5,000,000. but the sections are silent as to the ownership, except that in this section relating to working expenditure, it is provided that the Grand Trunk Pacific can add to the working expenditure any sum that they pay for the hire of rolling stock, let to the company as part of the equipment of the said eastern division. If the case were to go before a judge and the Minister of Justice were to say that ' equip ' means ' purchase and equip,' would not the judge say at once : You yourself have defined it in this clause which provides that they may lease a part of the equipment of the eastern division ? Is it open to question that it would be held that the requirements of the clause would be fulfilled by borrowing or leasing rolling stock for this division to the value of $5,000,000 ?
There is another consideration that the hon. gentleman will not overlook, that is the question of working expenses is for the first ten years. After that time we are not concerned with the working expenses. It is when the company has to pay rent that working expenses is allowed. We find that the company has to supply $5,000,000 worth of rolling stock for the eastern division, and because the government is satisfied that the business will not pay for ten years, they let them off from paying rent for ten years. When we find this state of affairs admitted by the government, would it not be the height of absurdity to say that while they will not make enough money to pay their rent, they will also be supposed to lease additional stock in addition to the $5,000,000? If that had been the case we can depend upon it that some of the shrewd lawyers who drew up this agreement would have put in two or three words here such as ' in addition to the $5,000,000 purchased therefor ' or words to that effect. Now, the Minister of Justice will say :	You have not
touched the 35th clause. Let tis read It. It provides for security in the shape of a mortgage which will be a first charge upon the railway, undertaking, equipment and property, tolls, rights and franchises of the company, including all equipment and property to be thereafter acquired by the company. If the company buys one car, the government it entitled to a mortgage on that car. If the company leases $5,000,000 worth

of equipment, what will be the effect; every lawyer knows that the lessee obtains a title which he can mortgage. That is the first charge on the lessee's interest. It would be a novel statement of law that the lessee could give a mortgage to be a charge on somebody else's property. The Minister of Justice must not forget that if the Grand Trunk Company feels so friendly to this Grand Trunk Pacific Company that they will guarantee their bonds gratuitously, they might possibly lease their cars on such favourable terms that if the government had to take over this road it would be an advantage to the government to step in and to take the lessees' position, and not compel them to buy new cars, but to use the old cars. But that is a different proposition from saying that because you are to have a mortgage upon equipment, you will have a mortgage upon the property of somebody else. Then when we take the other clauses (b), (c) and (d) they do not carry the subject any further. You come back to the equipment, and the moment you decide what equipment means then all these subsections follow naturally in their place.
Another argument the hon. gentleman made is that clause 37 is conclusive. I did not think he would refer to clause 37, but that he would have left a less skilful lawyer to refer to that. Now, here is a clause different from all other clauses in the contract. It is put in for a spec'fic purpose, and every one knows that purpose. It is put in to ensure that whatever the company buys in the construction and equipment of its road, it should buy in Canada. I do not think a more futile clause was ever put in any agreement by any conveyancer. All that Is provided is that the company shall purchase all material and supplies required for the construction of the western division and the equipment of the whole line, from Canadian producers when the same are produced in Canada, and when such materials and supplies can be purchased in desired quantities arid of equal quality for the purpose required and for prices and upon terms equally advantageous with those procurable elsewhere. That is to say, if the company can buy goods in Canada just as cheaply and of as good quality as they can out of Canada, they will be wise enough to save their freight and insurance and buy them at home. But if they do not choose to buy them in Canada there is no provision by which they can be compelled to do so, and who will be able to say in years to come that the contention of the company relying on this option, was wrong ? That is the purpose of that clause, to provide that what the company has to buy must be bought in Canada. What has that to do with the construction and equipment ? The word ' equipment ' stands by itself. If that implies that they must buy it in Canada, you do not need that clause; it is all provided for in the 22nd clause if equipment includes the idea of 284
purchase, if equipment does not include the idea of purchase, then this clause does not apply. So I submit that the contention raised by the leader of the opposition and my hon. friend from Hamilton is quite correct, and that this document does not provide the security that should be provided for the people of this country.
Then the Minister of Justice spoke about the country not being bound to pay anything until the road was completed. Now, I think he has not carefully read the clauses, or he would find that practically the government must contribute as the road goes on. 1 admit that it is optional.
I did not contend any more than that.

I think the hon. gentleman did, for this reason; unless he did contend for more than that, it was vain to speak of it at all. The only object would be to lead the people to believe that the country is not bound to pay while the road is being built. It is one thing to say the country is legally bound to pay, I do not say that; it is another thing to say the country is practically bound to pay, and that is what I do say. If this country is guaranteeing the bonds on $75,000,000, when it saw this company crippled by extortionate charges made on every contract, why should it not advance the money in the meantime Y Why, if the government exercised its option and did not pay a cent until the road was completed, that road would cost three or four times as much as it would if the contractors were paid as they went along. It would be interesting, when the hon. gentleman is again addressing the House, if he would enlighten us as to how the western section is to be built, assuming that the government pays nothing, guarantees no bonds, until the whole road is built.
I want to say a few words about the contract itself. It is such an extraordinary document that we are almost justified in declining to consider it on account of the inherent signs of weakness on almost every page of it. In the first place, it is indicative of haste, and perhaps that is the reason the Prime Minister said we must move at once, that there is no time for deliberation. If there has been one statement made in this debate that can be accepted by the House without hesitation, it is the statement that the government moved without deliberation. Perhaps one reason is that the government themselves did not know where they stood nor with whom they were dealing when they came to draw up a document for the construction of a transcontinental railway. When one looks at the original Bill, No. 64, to incorporate the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, it is seen that the incorporators are:	[DOT]

Cox, H. M. Pellatt. and E. R. Wood, all of Toronto, Ontario, the Honourable William Gibson, of Beamsville, On-



tario, J. R. Booth, ot Ottawa, Ontario, the Honourable H. B. Rainville, Charles M. Hays, Frank W. Morse and William Wainwright, all of Montreal, and John Bell of Belleville, together with such persons as become shareholders in the company, are incorporated under the name of ' The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway i Company,' hereinafter called ' the company.'
These gentlemen applied to parliament and we gravely discussed tlieir application in this House and passed the Bill which has gone to the Senate, but which has not been adopted there, incorporating these gentlemen as the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Then, suddenly, like a bolt out of the blue, comes down the government Bill setting forth that :
An agreement has been entered into, bearing date the 29th day of July, 1903, between His Majesty the King, of the first part, and Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson, C.B.,	G.C.M.G., and
others, representing therein and acting on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company-	[DOT]
Who are they ? The preamble tells us- -a company incorporated by an Act of the parliament of Canada passed at the present session thereof.
They are not incorporated, and the Act is not true on its face. This may be a small matter, but it shows the recklessness and the haste with which everything in connection with this contract has been done. It appears to me that the government apparently drew the Bill and the railway lawyers drew the contract When we look at the contract we find that it is between the government and a number of gentlemen-
Representing therein and acting on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, a company to be incorporated by an Act of the parliament of Canada passed at the present session thereof.
Showing that the railway lawyers knew the true position of affairs and that the government did not. I think it is rather extraordinary that this debate has proceeded for so long a time. The right hon. leader of the government has introduced this Bill, several of his colleagues have spoken but none of them has yet explained how it is that when eight or ten gentlemen apply in the ordinary course to' be incorporated, suddenly, liking the melting of the dew in the morning sun, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company disappears and we enter into a contract with several other gentlemen representing the Grand Trunk Railway Company and professing to represent the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Surely the House is entitled to an explana-tio.i as to the way in which this contract was drawn and as to why the government did not know the status of the gentlemen with whom they were dealing. Now, I will refer to section 21 of the Bill which is a peculiar section :
The Governor in Council shall have the power at any time to suspend the progress of tho

work upon the said eastern division until the then next session of parliament.
Is it possible that hon. gentlemen opposite have suspicions themselves ? Is it possible that they fear that what the hon. ex-i Minister of Railways and Canals says is right ? Is it possible that they anticipate, that the expenditure may be so enormous that even this country will not stand the construction of the eastern division, or is it possible that this agreement may be held before the country until after the election when the government can put in another division if they see fit ? Surely some light upon the subject should be given to an anxious and inquiring House. The hon. Minister of Justice has spoken of the care that has been exercised by the government to see that the road is constructed in a reasonable way. The hon. gentleman makes a fair presentment of the case. He points out that the government will construct the eastern division of the railway, that the company will pay 3 per cent on the cost of the railway, that the company will construct the western division of the railway, the government guaranteeing 75 per cent of the cost and that each will thereby be overlooking tlie line constructed by the other. He points out that in this way the country has been safeguarded. What could be safer, he asks ? How could any of the moneys-of the country be improperly expended where the interests of both parties are so carefully safeguarded? Let us look at section 7 and see how far they have been safeguarded. I would like to know whether the hon. Minister of Justice or the lawyers of the railway company are responsible for this clause :
In order to ensure, for the protection of the company as lessees of the eastern division of the said railway, the economical construction thereof in such a manner that it can be operated to the best advantage, it is hereby agreed

What do the people get as their security ? -that the specifications

That the specifications-the specifications

-for the construction of the eastern division shall be submited'to, and approved of by, the company before the commencement of the work.
What about the tenders ? What about the contracts ? Where does the money come in in the specifications ? It comes in with the tenders or the contracts. I think that the hon. gentlemen opposite must surely have thought that the people were worthy subjects of Barnum's irony when he said that the. people liked to be humbugged when he tells us about the provisions made for safeguarding the country, because, although he does provide for the specifications he makes no provision for the tenders and contracts and practically all the unholy work is done, if it is done at all, in connection with the tenders aud contracts. The same thing applies

to the western division. We read all through that there is such a provision in respect to the specifications, but not in regard to the tenders and contracts. I notice all through this agreement that one of the inherent weaknesses of the agreement is the careless and reckless manner in which it has been entered into. It is rather singular that we should be told by hon. gentlemen opposite that we are not to be put to any expense in connection with the construction of the eastern division because the Grand Trunk Pacific is to pay us a rental of 3 per cent. We guarantee their bonds for 3 per cent, but the bonds are payable half yearly, and the rental is payable yearly. It would have been the simplest thing in the world for the government to have insisted that if they have to pay the interest half yearly they should get the rent half yearly, because, in large sums running up into millions, a half year's interest represents a considerable amount of money. If the contract were drawn in the interest of the railway company it would have been drawn exactly in the way in which it has been drawn but if it were drawn in the interest of the country it would have been drawn in such a manner as to provide that the reiital should be paid half yearly. Then, there is another clause which provides that if the rent is not paid when due it is capitalized but it is not capitalized in such a way as to give compound interest to the country. There may be arrears that will be capitalized three years hence but the country will lose the interest in the meantime. Then clause 21 is a singular one. It provides that the state of affairs shall be at the end of the term :
If, upon the termination of the said lease, the government shall determine not to undertake the operation of the eastern division, tha company, provided the terms offered by it are as favoufable to the government as those offered by any other railway company equally competent to perform and fulfil the obligations required by the government to be assumed by the lessees thereof shall have the right to an extension or renewal of the said lease for a further period of fifty years, upon such terms as may be agreed upon.
I think any one will see that this puts the government in an extraordinary position. At the end of the time the government will be found operating the road from Moncton to Winnipeg beginning nowhere and ending nowhere. If they want to expropriate the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway running to the coast they can do it, but they would have to pay for the value of the road fifty years hence. Now they contribute three-quarters of what it will cost to build it, but they will have to pay the enhanced value that will accrue to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Pacific. No other company can possibly compete with the Grand Trunk Pacific, for the lease of the eastern division, because, suppose that any other company makes as good a proposition to operate the 2841
road the Grand Trunk Pacific by reason of the efficiency of its system, its connection with and its management of the eastern division would be in a better position to carry out the lease than any other railway company and therefore practically the government are making a present of the eastern section of this road to the Grand Trunk Pacific for all time to come, and should the government want to buy out the western section fifty years from now they will have to pay what the road is worth at that time. The government have contended that one of their chief reasons for carrying through this scheme is to secure the regulation of rates, but Che whole section, which purports to do this really appears to do everything else. If they expect to do it in the way in which the section relating to that matter is drawn I would say that it is the surest way to avoid the accomplishment of the result which they profess to have in view. Just look for a moment at the position of the farmers of this country. We have $25,000,000 of one kind of stock, and we have $20,000,000 of another kind of stock that will be given among the promoters and the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway for nothing, and for all time to come the farmers of the North-west must make sacrifices to pay dividends on this stock which is given to some one for nothing. And yet, this is supposed to be in the interest of this country.
I am not prepared to go so far as to advocate the building of a road from Moncton to the Pacific as a government road, although perhaps the time may come when with further information, and because of changes in the conditions of the country, I might be willing to go thus far. But, Sir, I have no hesitation in saying, that as between a scheme to which the government is to contribute 75 per cent of the money for a certain time, taking all the risks, and the company supplying nothing, but getting a friend to guarantee for 25 per cent, and taking all the profits ; I say unhesitatingly that in the interests of the people of this country we had better own the road and hold the $25,000,000 pref erred stock and the other millions of common stock, as trustees for the people of the country, than have outsiders drawing dividends on these stocks for1 50 years to come.
I do not intend to occupy the time of the House longer, save to call attention to one point, and I call attention to that mainly in order to illustrate the style of argument that hon. gentlemen opposite have adopted. If hon. gentlemen would only honestly face the facts and reason from them, perhaps there would not be as great difference of opinion between the two sides of the House as we often find. Let me take one illustration. The Minister of the Interior went Into ecstacies on the one hand, and was filled with amazement and 'horror on the other.

because gentlemen on this side of tbe House praised Mr. Booth for what he had done, and blamed the government for what they had done. That would be a perfectly fair and reasonable argument if Mr. Booth and the government had done the same thing, but it is a perfectly unreasonable argument and an insult to the intelligence of the House, if Mr. Booth andi the government had not done the same thing. What are the facts ? Mr. Booth had a line and the government had a line ; Mr. Booth had his own Canada Atlantic Railway and the government had their own Intercolonial Railway ; Mr. Booth decided to extend his line. The first thing he did was to make the surveys, to lay out the plans and locate the line, and after he had made his surveys and located the line, then he decided to build. Did the government do that T I>o we not find fault with the government on that point beyond most others, that what Mr. Booth did, they did not do, because they did not make such surveys? Then when Mr. Booth got ready to build he extended his own line,
Let me ask the hon. gentleman, if Mr. Booth has surveyed the line that he is now proposing to build from Whitney west, and for which he has obtained a charter ?

I am speaking of the Canada Atlantic Railway extension to Depot Harbour, which was alluded to by the Minister of the Interior, and I am trying to show the vast difference in the circumstances under which Mr. Booth built his road to Depot Harbour, and the circumstances under which the government propose to build this road through an unknown land. Mr. Booth extended his own line. Is the government extending its line? Mr. Booth, by extending his line, improved and increased the value of his line. The government is not extending their line, they are paralleling their line. Surely there is a difference there. We may well bless Mr. Booth and blame the government as to that. Then, after Mr. Booth had built his line as an extension of his own line, he operated his line. I am not aware that the government propose to operate the line that they are going to spend so much money to construct. Then, after Mr. Booth had constructed his line he carried all his freight by his new line over the full length of the new line down to the old, and he had the additional benefit not merely of the carriage of the freight on the new line, but the additional profits from its carriage on the old. The government are not doing that; they are handing over their line to another company. Then, when Mr. Booth was looking about for a place to extend his line, he extended it to the lakes ; that is along the line suggested by the leader of the opposition. Mr. Booth extended his line where he knew he could get business ; he

extended it to the place where people were looking for it, and where they brought their grain for transport. Has the government extended its line to the lakes ? Have they not built a blind line to Winnipeg, where they get nothing except what comes from this other line which is projected as a continuation of it across the prairies ? I think it is a reasonable conclusion that when this side of the House applauded Mr. Booth for what he did, they could not help but to blame the government for what they did. We were consistent in applauding Mr. Booth and blaming the government, because what that sane, sensible, shrewd, business man, Mr. Booth did to make his road a success, has been carefully avoided by the government, and that is the reason they are going to make their scheme such a failure.
We appeal to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House to recognize that this is a question which should rise above party politics. No one will deny for a moment that the expenditure of from $100,000,000 to $150,000,000 must affect the credit of this country for better or for worse. No one will deny that the expenditure of $100,000,000 or $150,000,000 on this proposed railway will certainly curtail other expenditures which may be more desirable and more important in the future than the construction of this railway. And, Sir, I appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite at such a time as this, to lay aside party prejudices, to look on the question simply on its merits, to decline to be automatic voting machines, to refuse to jump like jacks in the box simply because the Prime Minister may pull the strings, but as intelligent representatives of the people to recognize that they owe a duty to their country and to those who sent them here. I appeal to them to consider the reasons which have been given by the ministry to support of the measure, and if they find that no one of the reasons given is founded on fact, if they find that few of the guarantees promised are found in existence, I ask them to join with this side of the House in defeating this measure, and allowing the country to obtain the best return it possibly can for the money it may expend on the solution of the transportation problem.

, I desire Mr. Speaker, to say a few words on this very important question. I do not think it necessary that I should offer any apology, even though I may uot be able to make my remarks as interesting as many hon. gentlemen who preceded me, or who may come after me. But, Sir, having occupied a position in public life for so long a time, having witnessed the Initiation of the Intercolonial Railway as well as the initiation of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and having lived to see these two great projects accomplished facts, I do feel a deep interest

as a Canadian-which is the proper interest to feel-in this great national project. I feel a special interest on this occasion coming as I do from the province of New Brunswick, because at no time in the history of this country since confederation, have the interests of New Brunswick been so much exposed to misrepresentation and prejudice. I feel it my duty therefore, Sir, to repudiate many of the statements made during this debate. This whole discussion has been in many respects extraordinary. Gentlemen who spoke in opposition to the scheme have from the beginning condemned this policy, and have condemned the government for introducing it, because' as they allege, there is no proper data before us. We have been told by gentlemen who have spoken against this project, that the country in New Brunswick west of Moncton is absolutely unknown,	that the	northern parts of
Quebec and Ontario are also unknown, and the same argument is applied all along the line. But, Sir, any one listening to the discussion must be surprised at the assertions which these gentlemen make as to a total absence of information on the part of the government when you think of the full and complete information, which these gentlemen themselves say they are possessed of, as to the heavy grades to be encountered, the mountains to be crossed, and the difficulties to be overcome. If there is a total absence of information, how is it that there is so much information to prejudice the scheme ? I think the two arguments are inconsistent-just as inconsistent as many of the other points taken. The Intercolonial Railway was an important factor in the question of confederation, so important that without that inducement to the maritime provinces, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick would not. I believe, have entered into the confederation at that time. Since confederation and since the construction of the Intercolonial Railway, I have sat here under both administrations, and I have heard the attempt frequently made, especially in the province of Ontario, 'to prejudice the members coming from that section against the Intercolonial Railway as a burthen on the people of Ontario for the special benefit of the people of the maritime provinces. I think that was a most unfair and ungenerous charge to make. In the first place, the principle was laid down from the start, that there was no idea that the Intercolonial Railway should be constructed as a commercial line. It was for the purpose of uniting the different provinces, encouraging interprovincial trade, and bringing the people together. We in the western section of the province-and I include the city of St. John and all the counties along the river in that section-felt that our interests were sacrificed by the adoption of the Robinson route: and we are told today that we are responsible because the
route was not a commercial success. We are not responsible. The selection was made from a military point of view, and but for that consideration the Robinson route would never have been adopted. Hon. gentlemen may talk as they please, but those who remember the discusions before confederation and in the first session of parliament after confederation, will admit, I am sure, that the arguments were overwhelming in favour first, of the frontier route, as it was called, and secondly, the central route as a compromise. We have been told by hon. gentlemen, in this debate, and by a newspaper which has been cautiously discussing this scheme, in its issue of the 15th of August, that the central portion of New Brunswick is an impassable section of country. More than that, some hon. members have said that it is a worthless country, not worth developing. I do not feel that I have any great cause of complaint against these hon. gentlemen, because the hon. ex-Min-istey of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair), the one representative in the cabinet from our province, has indicated in his speech that the road will pass through a country difficult and almost worthless, leaving out the better portions which are settled. Now, Mr. Speaker, so far as the position of the hon. ex-Minister of Railways is concerned, I have been a friend, politically speaking, of that hon. gentleman for a great many years. I supported him as the leader of a coalition government in our province, which lasted for years to the satisfaction of both parties in the province. I supported him then while he was a Liberal, as I have supported him while he was a minister in the present government. I have no desire to say one word that would be offensive to that hon. gentleman or his many friends. But I have a right to say this, that when the hon. gentleman, who represents the province of New Brunswick in the cabinet, gave the reasons why he retired from the government and condemned this policy-and I say it in all candour and in all honour-that I have not yet heard any reason given by that hon. gentleman that satisfies me that it was the reason which induced him to take that step. The hon. gentleman himself, in discussing this question, has taken the ground, as have all the newspapers which have attacked this scheme, that the weak point in it is the eastern extension of the line from Quebec to Moncton. Why, it was first assailed as the result of piratical efforts on the part of the maritime members; and if we find ourselves weak in that respect, it is because the hon. ex-Minister of Railways has given strength to that argument. But we are only weak because arguments which have no foundation in fact are used against that part of the scheme. The hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart). who always speaks as a practical man, and who has himself had a large experience as Minister of Railways-though he sometimes speaks

without being sure of his facts-stated his objections to the extension of that eastern section from Quebec to Moncton. First, he stated that it would merely be a parallel road-that for the first 100 miles after leaving Ldvis it would not be more than fifteen miles from the Intercolonial Railway at any one point. I am sure that if the hon. gentleman will look into the facts, he will be the first to see that he has made a mistake. At no point after the road leaves Chau-diere Junction will it be within double that distance of the Intercolonial until it passes that point in Maine so often referred to on the St. Francis river. From that point it increases the distance until it more than doubles and trebles it, and, as was well stated by the Prime Minister, it passes through a country which is quite inaccessible by the Intercolonial, and is separated from it by that range of mountains which in fact has been used a$ an argument against the construction of this road-as if this road would cross over those mountains. We do not generally build railways over mountains. If these ridges were impassable mountains, with no breaks or natural valleys in them, I would admit that there was something in that argument. But nature has solved the problem. Do you think you are going to traverse the Rocky Mountains with a railway because it is said they are insuperable and you cannot build a practicable line over them ? That is true, but nature has solved that problem in many cases. You have the Kicking Horse pass, the Yellow Head pass, the Pine River pass, the Peace River pass. The wTaters in that pass rise wfithin 125 miles of the Pacific coast. Its waters rise in the hills and flow eastward through thousands of square miles of that territory, which lies beyond the Rocky Mountains, and find their passage through the main range of the Rocky Mountains, continue on eastward forming the Peace river, thence to Athabaska and Greater Slave lakes and into the Mackenzie river, and on to the Arctic ocean. That is on account of the natural formation there, and the question of grades does not arise at all. Other passes are south of that.
I listened to the hon. gentleman from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes), a gentleman who has attained such a reputation for his military capacities, who has such high ideals, if not great ambitions, in that direction, who excels in everything he undertakes; and he produced the most wonderful results by merely glancing over the country. I am sure he never travelled all the country he has spoken of, but everywhere he went through that portion of New Brunswick and up through Quebec, as he travelled in his imagination along that route- because he never actually travelled over it-the hills and mountains were rolling around him and getting higher and higher, until it was a question to my mind which Hon. Mr. COSTIGAN.
was the most elevated-these mountain peaks or the hon. gentleman himself.
The doubt is in favour of the hon. gentleman.

The proposed route, so far as I know-and I shall not undertake to assert things I have not a reasonable knowledge of-from Chaudiere Junction will not cross the height of land where any of these altitudes which have been referred to occur. It will avoid the height of land by following up the valleys of the streams which fall into the St. Lawrence. Passing by that' range of mountains, it will cross one or two small tributaries which flow into the St. John, it will reach the south side of that range of mountains and follow down until it comes to that point near the boundary lake, where it joins the River St. Francis. The general report on our rivers is that the difference in levels is about ten feet in the mile. There can be no very great difficulty where the difference does not exceed ten feet per mile, and it does not in the river I have mentioned. You go down that valley, you strike the valley of the St. John in Canadian territory, and go on to Edmundston and Grand Falls, and thence strike across the country to Moncton. My own impression is that the final location would be via Edmundston and Grand Falls, but that is a matter of detail to be settled later. The engineering difficulties held out against the scheme are bugbears, and have no existence outside the imaginations of gentlemen who used them as arguments. We are told that the surveys made by Sir Sandford Fleming, or under his direction, prove absolutely that it is impossible to get through that central portion of New Brunswick. Well, while the report is not very favourable, what is it ? It says that the central portion of New Brunswick is an assemblage of high hills running up the sources of the Tobique, the Miramichi, the Restigouche and the Upsal-quitch. It is true that all the rivet's named rise in a small area, and flow in different directions, and that in that section, where these rivers take their source, you have a cluster of hills of considerable elevation; and if any one spoke of getting a road through there, I would say, not that it was impracticable, but that there were heavy grades, and that the greatest trouble would be the curvature and the length of line. But the proposed line goes south of all these highlands. The highest of the whole range in that province is the Blue Mountain, on the north-east, side of the Tobique river, about 40 or 45 miles from its junction with the St. John river. If any one were to tell me that the government had decided to build a road across the Blue Mountain, I would say that the government did not know much about the country,

and I would urge them to seek bettor information.
If you built from Riviere du Loup, you would have to cross the Blue Mountain.

No. There is a road built from Riviere du Loup to Edmundston now and in operation. When the debate was on with regard to the question of finally locating the Intercolonial Railway, we were pretty evenly divided in New Brunswick between the valley route and the north shore route, so that our vote did not amount to much. We always believed that Nova Scotia would favour the Robinson route, because that would place it in a more advantageous position towards St. John than If the road went down the valley of the St. John. I stated in my speech at nomination that the province of Quebec would naturally favour a route which would go down the St. Lawrence through Quebec counties and develop two of these counties, while the other route would not develop so many, and that the province of Ontario might be careless about the matter unless it were influenced by political reasons. But importance was attached to the military consideration, and what turned the scales was the fact that we had the credit of the English government for the cost of the construction of the road at that time, on condition that the British government approved the route adopted. That route was built, and the feeling in New Brunswick was this: While the people were disappointed, while they felt that a road three times more expensive, a great deal longer, less commercial in its aspect was selected, still people in the western portion, in course of time, did not begrudge the road to the north shore people, and the general opinion has been that after all it was as well, because a railway was afterwards constructed in that valley, in the local interest, up as far as Edmundston, and the north shore would not have got its road had it to depend on its own resources.
The impression left on the minds of hon. gentlemen who spoke from the opposition side, judging from their speeches, was that the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals left the government because he could not support that scheme conscientiously, because it was a wild, inconsiderate and ill-considered scheme. But he did not leave the cabinet, as I understand it, because the government refused to take his view and go to St. John for a shorter road. That would have been inconsistent with the ground he took himself and the ground he is given the credit of having taken. His whole ground was that he could not justify the paralleling of the Intercolonial Railway. No one will say that a shorter line than the one now proposed could be found by going from Riviere du Loup across Temiscouata to Edmundston and down by the valley of St. John.	,
Surely no one in this House will say that the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals resigned his seat in the government because the Intercolonial was to be paralleled, and destroyed, and dismantled, and discredited, and that he would have remained a defender of that policy if they had only paralleled the road by going along the Temiscouata route to St. John instead of to Moncton ? That would be inconsistent. But there is an object in having the two strings to the bow. That object appears in a newspaper published in New Brunswick, the St. John ' Telegraph.' The ' Telegraph ' indicates that the hon. minister left the government when he found that the government would not agree to the construction of a road across from the Intercolonial at Riviere du Loup to Edmundston and down the valley of St. John to St. John. That is not honest politics at all. But what would be the value of such a road ? You have heard the objections to the grades and curvatures and the cost of construction of the proposed route. I do not profess to be a railway engineer, but I profess to have a little practical knowledge and to be able to form opinions as to what conclusions practical men like myself might draw from certain facts. I can tell this House that a road was built from Riviere du Loup to Edmundston, largely subsidized by this parliament. It has been in operation for years. It was built in the face of reports against the grades and curvatures of that route. A firm by the name of Fraser & Son, Scotchmen, who came to New Brunswick and settled in that country and succeeded in building up a lumbering and milling business, bought the limits and put up a mill, one of the largest in New Brunswick, on the shores of Lake Temiscouata, half way between Rivi6re du Loup and Edmundston. They made a contract with the company to deliver the lumber at RiviSre du Loup for shipment. I do not know what the grades are, but I know that, with a load of ten cars, the engine has to do a great deal of puffing to pull the train over the line; and I know that if you put more than ten cars on a train you have to put on two engines. You do not require to study what the grades are; you see the effects of the grades. You could not make a profitable freight road out of that. Besides it would be 40 miles longer than the proposed road even to Edmundston, without counting the saving from Edmundston across the province to Moncton.
I shall not attempt to go into the matter of the contract or the legal conditions. I think that some of the lay members of this House are quite capable of taking part in a discussion of that kind and holding their own pretty well with the legal gentlemen. But I think it would be undesirable for me to interfere. I am satisfied that the gentlemen who are looking after the interests of the government, and to the interest of the country, are reliable men and capable of

guarding the public interest, as it is their duty to do. And, without saying anything offensive, I ana not at all convinced that the gentlemen who criticise the contract are satisfied that that contract is as worthless as they appear to make out. I am satisfied that it is worthy of the support of this House. Some hon. gentlemen have said what would happen if you could get the voice of the people upon it. 1 can look ibagk as one of the men who stood here over twenty years ago, when, after the acquisition of the North-west Territories and the bringing in of British Columbia, Sir John Macdonald proposed the policy of the Canadian Pacific Railway transcontinental line, as it was then considered. I followed the speech of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) the other evening with great interest. I thought it was one of the good speeches of this debate-argumentative and full of information. But the last part did not, in my opinion strengthen his argument, nor was it necessary to his case. I myself will make a comparison between the two contracts and the two enterprises, this one and the Canadian Pacific Railway. My object will be to prove that the Canadian people are as ready to-day to endorse the policy of the government in this scheme as they were to endorse the policy of the government at that time. I do not think it is necessary or in good taste to undertake to prove that that contract was not a good one. The country has decided that question long ago. The Canadian Pacific Railway has aided to build up this country more than anything else that has been done-we are at one on that point. But let us make a fair comparison of the two enterprises. When Sir John Macdonald entered upon his bold policy based upon his hope and confidence in the future of this country more than anything else, there was no very full information as to the capabilities of the North-west Territories, nor was there much confidence in its capabilities, but one thing largely strengthened that policy, and that was that, having brought in British Columbia, having acquired the North-west Territories, there was only one way to administer them as a part of the Dominion, and that was to build the railway. We could only hope that the railway would justify its own construction- and it did amply. The government o.f the day had to give large subsidies in money, in land, and in constructed railways, in order to get the company to undertake that contract. It has 'been said that the terms were extravagant. Anyone who can remember the debate of that day knows that there was severe criticism, and perhaps as unreasonable and unwarranted criticism as there is against this scheme to-day. If any one is inclined to think that that was an extravagant contract let him remember these two things. First that the land that was given at that time was worthless if it was not developed by the construction of that road ;

and second that after that company was organized, entered upon its contract, made its financial arrangements, and commenced operations, it had to come back to parliament and say : We cannot go on, we are at the end of our resources; the whole thing is up unless we get a loan of $30,000,000 from the Canadian parliament. That staggered the Canadian people, the members of parliament and even the members of the government. But, Sir John Macdonald found that it was a necessary and safe investment to make. He made the loan. It secured the construction of this great work, and every dollar of the loan was paid pack. I feel proud of having contributed to that great work. I feel proud to have lived long enough to give my vote, and as I intend to do, in favour of the great work which is now proposed. And, while I would not like to hear an hon. member decry the result or the terms of the policy of building the Canadian Pacific Railway, I am going to try to do what is fair by this policy in a comparison of the two. When that land was given to encourage the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, it was worthless. It has become of great value now. When the contract was entered into the faith in the future and the confidence of success was more limited than the prospects of the success of this enterprise. Cannot this government go to the people of Canada to-day and say : You endorsed the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway originally to develop the North-west and British Columbia. You did not know what you were undertaking at that time. It was a courageous undertaking. But to-day you have the country partially developed, and when I say partially developed, I have in view the almost boundless extent of that country. You propose to build another line there. Why ? Because the lands that were unknown then are known now, not only to the Canadian government and people, but to the civilized world. Those lands are known now to be capable of producing enough bread to feed not only Canada but millions of people across the Atlantic. They are known to be valuable lands, bringing good prices.
One good feature about this scheme is that it will pass through undeveloped portions of that territory and will increase the value of the lands just in the same proportion that the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway increased the value of the lands in the sections through which it passes. But there will be this difference, that while the Canadian Pacific Railway were entitled to the lands that they earned, they are at the same time reaping a rich harvest in the value of these lands that were of unknown value twenty years ago. The lands which will be increased in value by the construction of this road will not pass into the hands of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, but will remain the property

of Canada for Canadian settlers. I think you should not underestimate that one feature of this contract. I do not say this for the purpose of making a contrast to the prejudice of the former contract. You could not have constructed the first line in that way, because there was no such guarantee of the future value of the land as there is now. Therefore you are fully justified in undertaking tills expenditure, which is moderate after all compared with the results to lie achieved.
Some one has said : Who has asked for a transcontinental line ? Where is the hurry for this line ? Why, Sir, three years ago this question was discussed in this parliament, and it has been discussed since ; it has been discussed by the press throughout the country. Now this question of transportation is no doubt at the present time the chief question before the Canadian people, and it is worthy all their attention. It should be considered, as my hon. friend who preceded me suggested, on broad Canadian lines, independent of party considerations. This great question is coupled with another one of great importance. The solution of the transportation problem also carries with it a development to the largest possible extent of the Dominion of Canada. You cannot introduce a scheme into this country and call it a Canadian scheme if it leaves any portion of the Canadian people out in the cold, let them be little or big, few or numerous. That was the policy at the bottom of confederation, that is why the Intercolonial was built, that is why the Canadian Pacific Railway was built later- to cement together all the provinces between the two oceans. Therefore I say the scheme promises not only to solve the transportation question, but to do for Canada more than could be done in any other way by developing all the provinces of the Dominion. In the west you develop new lands all through that enormous region, you develop trade for British Columbia, you develop a hew field for the mining industry of British Columbia, you develop a new outlet for timber industries, you develop agricultural lauds that so far have been inaccessible. You do the same to a considerable extent for the province of Manitoba. Then you come down through northern Ontario and develop sections there of immense value to that old province, and without a cent of cost directly to that province except its proportionate share of the general cost. You come to Quebec, and you develop the northern portion of that province. I have heard some hon. gentlemen from the province of Quebec say that this is a barren country through which the railway is to run. Well. I would advise them not to say that too often, because the reports do not justify the statement, and we may conclude that the argument is used more for political effect than in the interest of the province.
Now, Sir, the name of the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals is used, and his authority is given for the assertion that the part of New Brunswick to be developed by this line is a barren waste. Well, I am going to make a statement on my word as a member of parliament, and I know more of that country than any other man inside this House or outside of it, and that is saying a good deal, though I am not given to boasting. I have travelled through the most of that country, I have surveyed part of that country for farm lots, in the county of Carleton adjoining my own constituency. I have fished, I have hunted, I have cruised. I have lumbered through that country, and I make the statement defying contradiction, that this country is a valuable section of country. I do not say that it will compare with the prairie section, I do not say that it will compare with the Niagara peninsula, but I do say that we cannot find in the Dominion of Canada an equal extent of wilderness lands still unsettled of greater value than this very tract that is decried to-day. I make that statement knowing whereof I speak. The upper portion of it will compare favourably with any highland in Canada, no matter how fertile it is. It has some of the finest land you can imagine. In the county of Victoria and the Mada-waska region you will find highlands and bushlands of the greatest value. After that country had been surveyed into lots, you could tell a man : Go to the Crown lands office and take a map, and pick out any number you like ; you cannot miss it, they are all alike. Now you cannot do that in every country, for you would be liable to get a waste lot, to get a swamp lot. That extends down through the counties of Madawaska, Victoria. Carleton and York. From York across to Moncton the land will not average as high, but it is good agricultural land, and it is well timbered. When I say well timbered I do not mean to contradict one statement that was made especially by the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals. One of the points made by that lion, gentleman was that the valuable timber had all been taken out of the country. There is a good deal of truth in that, but there are gentlemen here who know something about the lumberman's business, gentlemen who have not been engaged in the business but who will easily understand that when lumbering operations are carried on in territories adjacent to streams and natural watercourses which are convenient for transporting the lumber from the country the lumber can be floated down these streams and they get the benefit of these watercourses, but beyond the region of these streams there is no other outlet and the timber remains there. Practical business men in this House and in the country well know that under the conditions in a country like that where the best lumber

has been taken out of the country and where the streams have been utilized as highways down which the raw material in the form of logs is taken, if you have a railway beyond that country you will develop new industries as important as the ones w7hich have been nearly exhausted, because you are reaching a point in the country which has hitherto not been reached by these lumbering operations and you are giving opportunities to do the most important work that can be done, that is to produce the finished article, or if not the absolutely finished article to add to its finished condition, or to approach the finished condition and to ship it in this form over the railway thus develoifing new interests in that section of the country besides developing the agricultural interests and these two interests combined are necessary one to the other in creating a trade for the railway that is running through the country. Fifty years ago there was talk of railway construction. You could not talk with the view of interesting any capitalist in a railway enterprise unless you brought before him statistics of good character, statistics that were undisputed that would show the probable trade that the road would do. Now it is a pretty generally accepted idea and principle that given an undeveloped country with any mineral resources, or lumber or agricultural capabilities, and put a road through it that road will develop new industries and thus bring the country into a condition of usefulness. X was very much struck also by the fact which was developed during the discussion that a man may even be led too far by Ms enthusiastic impulses. When the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals was talking of the capabilities of the Intercolonial Railway he used one argument that to my surprise was received with wonderful applause on this side of the House. I would not applaud it and for the reason that I would not have applauded it it should not have been applauded on this side of the House if it had been thoroughly understood. What was it ? In 1883, I think, Sir Charles Tupper came to this parliament and proposed a vote of $170,000 for a guarantee for 15 years to the Canadian Pacific Railway for the purpose of joining Montreal with St. John and Halifax. The project did not mature, but next year, in 1884, Sir Charles Tupper came down to the House again with a proposition to give $250,000, speaking from memory, or $280,000 for 20 years.

$250,000 for 20 years instead of $170,000 for 15 years. It was
not this time to join Montreal with St. John and Halifax, but this guarantee was given to' secure the construction of a road starting from the south side of the St. Lawrence, opposite Montreal, passing down through the townships to Moose Head Lake, Mat-tawamkeag, Fredericton and then to Salis-Hon.
