bury. It was a wTell defined route as far as it appeared in the resolution. What was the explanation which Sir Charles Tupper gave for paralleling the Intercolonial Railway, even if he had to go through a foreign country to do it ? Sir Charles Tupper stated that the Intercolonial Railway had been built for military purposes and for considerations other than commercial purposes and that it had done more than was expected of it by its friends and opponents, but on account of its mileage, the ports of St. John and Halifax could not be expected to compete against American ports unless some way was found to shorten the distance to St. John. It wras in order to shorten the distance to St. John by giving these better facilities for getting to St. John that the Intercolonial Railway was paralleled and it was intended that it should compete successfully. That was the point. We gave that large guarantee for this new road. It was built to St. John and not to Salisbury. What did the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals prove the other night and which I think was so strangely cheered ? He proved that Sir Charles Tupper's justification for giving $250,000 for 20 years for a short line was a mistake and then he said that Sir Charles Tupper was all wrong. After saying that Sir Charles Tupper was wrong in asking parliament to provide this, guarantee and that parliament was wrong in aiding the building of a short line as a successful competitor with the Intercolonial Railway he said :	I know that when the
cattle embargo was on the Intercolonial Railway carried cattle down to St. John quicker and cheaper than the short line could after all the expense they have gone to. What does that mean ? I think that Sir Charles Tupper's reasoning was good. What I am complaining of is the argument that Sir Charles Tupper having asked parliament to make this expenditure and having given reasons which are logical the fact which the hon. gentleman stated proves that the building of a short line was not a success. If it was not a success in this instance, it was because the grades and curvatures were too great. Now, I perhaps have spoken too long-half an hour-but I do not think half an hour is very long compared with the speeches that have been made on this side of the House, and I promised my hon. friends that I would not take the floor until short speeches became the order of the evening.
The order of the morning.

I will not take up much more of your time. We had hopes In the west of the province that at the time Sir Charles Tupper made the proposition some line like this proposed line would he found through Canadian territory shortening the distance to St. John. And our hopes were reasonably well founded, and I think they would have been realized had it not been for the fact of existing lines constructed then, reaching towards Mcose Head lake, and leaving the shorter distance to be constructed. To our western friends I would say that the transportation problem after all arises in that country. There is no doubt that the future welfare of Canada depends on the successful solution of that question. What the people of the west want is a cheaper outlet for their products, and no Canadian would be patriotic if he did not endeavour to secure for them that cheap outlet. We want their produce to come through Canadian territory to build up our ports in the east, as we will endeavour to help building up their country in the west. In that way the people of the west and the people of the east will have a common object in view. One hon. gentleman stated to-day that he took a broad position as a Canadian, and that he -spurned the idea of sectionalism. But he complained that the government were by this sclnin" pro itling a through line for freight so that the labourers along the route would get no toll out of it, and he pointed out to the member for Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy) that Collingwood was going to be destroyed by this policy. Well, that was not a very broad view of the case, because the proper Idea is to get as little toll as possible out of the western grain as it passes through Canada, and the labourers will be compensated In other ways than by* taking this toll.
In conclusion, I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that I have spoken on this subject chiefly because I know that there will be an effort to misrepresent this scheme, especially that part cf it which passes through the central part of New Brunswick, and which s me pretend to regard as the weak spot in the project. Well, Sir, I am sorry we have not the help of the ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) to promote the interests of New Brunswick on this'occasion. I am quite sure, however, that these gentlemen on the Conservative benches who now praise him so highly, would pepper him just as hotly if he were to open his mouth in favour of this project, or in favour of his province. He has risen high in the estimation of our friends of the opposition
very suddenly. He deserves their respect and good opinion. He is a capable and able man, but their attitude towards him has very quickly and very materially changed. I must express my deep sympathy however, with one old friend in this House, I refer to the energetic and talented member for St. Mary's (Hon. Sir. Tarte). When he ceased to be a minister of the Crown he was deified all at once by his former opponents, and instead of being in their eyes an avowed traitor to his country as they had termed him, he became the ablest minister that ever sat in the Laurier cabinet. His stock went up wonderfully ; he was received with open arms ; he was courted and complimented and flattered. But since-the ex-Slinister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) has appeared upon the scene, I notice that my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) seems to have dropped into oblivion There is not half the importance attached to him now that there was a few months ago, and lately the affection of the members of the opposition has been centred upon this greatest man that ever was at the head of the Railway Department. But, Sir, remember that these very same gentlemen are those who denounced the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) not so long ago as anything but honest or moral. I have to say that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair), has been a strong man in his province. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) made it a leading feature in his speech to attack the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) who is an old personal friend of mine, and a gentleman whom I have known for a great many years. The member for East Grey dealt with the member for Westmoreland without gloves, hut if he did not hurt the member for Westmoreland any more than he hurt the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway scheme, the member for Westmoreland will long survive.
I am sorry I killed him.

I do not suppose that the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) had any desire to injure my hon. friend physically, but I can tell him that any private member in this House might feel well satisfied to enjoy so highly the confidence of his constituents as does the hon. member for Westmoreland. It was also stated by some one that the hon. member for Westmoreland was the pupil or the protege of the exMinister of Railways: Let me say that the hon. member (Mr. Emmerson) is a strong man in his. county, and a strong man in his province. He is well known all through the province of New Brunswick, and is highly respected wherever he is known. Let no one make any mistake about the standing of the hon. member for Westmoreland in the province of New Brunswick. He is a gentleman of long experience, a gentleman with a good record, and a gentleman who is trusted among the people ot New Bruns-

wick. No one would be less disposed to minimize the good qualities of the ex-minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) than I, but after very considerable experience I can say that there is no man so strong that he can do without his friends, and whatever strength that bon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) had in this parliament he owes it to the good friends who have stood behind him. If they stand behind him yet, he is as strdng as ever, but if they do not support him, he will be very weak indeed, so far as federal influence is concerned. I myself have been pretty strong in my own county. I have fought a great many elections, and I have represented it a great many years. I suppose that even my opponents will say that I am a strong man in that county, but I would like to know how strong I would be if I lost the confidence of the men who make me strong. There is where the whole question comes in. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that I can speak for my own constituency, as there are other men to speak for theirs, and I can say unhesitatingly that so far as I can judge of other constituencies, without speaking officially for them, this scheme is well viewed in New Brunswick and will receive cheerful and strong support in that province.
